option_c: Keyword-Driven — tests are defined in spreadsheet keyword tables
option_d: Pure TDD — only unit tests are written before production code
explanation: It is a Hybrid framework: Data-Driven via Excel + parametrize, UI abstraction via POM, and test-first thinking from TDD.

subject: Pytest
question: What is the role of base_page.py in the framework?
option_a: A parent class all Page Objects inherit from, providing reusable methods like click(), send_keys(), is_visible(), and scroll_to_element() with built-in explicit waits
option_b: A test base that manages the browser lifecycle and captures screenshots on failure
option_c: A configuration reader that parses config.yaml and exposes environment settings
option_d: A data provider class that reads Excel test data and passes it to test scripts
explanation: base_page.py is the foundation of the POM layer; its generic interaction methods (with explicit waits) are shared by every page class, eliminating repetition.

subject: Pytest
question: What is conftest.py's role and why does Pytest discover it automatically?
option_a: It is the framework 'engine' — Pytest automatically reads it to share fixtures and hooks across all test files without explicit imports
option_b: It is the entry point that manually imports and registers every test file with Pytest
option_c: It is a base class that all test classes inherit from to access the browser driver
option_d: It is a configuration loader that reads pytest.ini settings at startup
explanation: Pytest's plugin mechanism automatically picks up conftest.py files, making their fixtures and hooks available to all tests in the same directory tree.

subject: Pytest
question: What fixture in conftest.py runs exactly once per session and creates the timestamped log folder?
option_c: pytest_configure, which is a hook function rather than a fixture
explanation: scope='session' means it runs once for the whole test session; autouse=True means no test needs to explicitly request it — it fires automatically.

subject: Pytest
question: What is the main responsibility of the setup_and_teardown fixture in base_test.py?
option_a: Launching a fresh browser before each test, closing it after, and capturing screenshots and logs for the Allure report on failure
option_b: Setting up the session-wide logger and creating the timestamped log directory
option_c: Reading config.yaml and initialising environment settings once per session
option_d: Registering custom markers and configuring the default Allure report directory path
explanation: setup_and_teardown is the test lifecycle manager: it provides a clean browser per test and ensures failure evidence (screenshots, logs) is attached to Allure.

subject: Pytest
question: What scope does the setup_and_teardown fixture in BaseTest use, and what does that mean?
option_a: scope='function' — it runs before and after every individual test function
option_b: scope='session' — it runs once at the very start and end of the entire test session
option_c: scope='class' — it runs once per test class, shared by all methods in that class
option_d: scope='module' — it runs once per test file regardless of method count
explanation: function scope ensures complete isolation: every test starts with a new browser and ends with a clean shutdown, preventing cross-test contamination.

subject: Pytest
question: What does a test class like TestLogin gain by inheriting from BaseTest?
option_a: Automatic browser setup and teardown per test via setup_and_teardown, plus Allure failure evidence capture
option_b: Access to all Excel test data from ExcelDataProvider without explicit imports
option_c: Automatic registration of custom markers with pytest.ini
option_d: Shared session_logger fixture that avoids re-creating log folders
explanation: Inheriting BaseTest means every test method in that class automatically gets a fresh driver, browser cleanup, and screenshot capture on failure — no boilerplate needed.

subject: Pytest
question: What are the two types of reports generated by this framework?
option_a: Allure Report (primary, interactive HTML with steps/logs/screenshots) and pytest-html (secondary, single self-contained HTML file)
option_b: JUnit XML (for CI/CD) and pytest-html (for sharing with stakeholders)
option_d: pytest-html (primary) and a custom CSV report (secondary)
explanation: Allure is the rich primary report; pytest-html is a lightweight secondary report that is easy to email or share as a single file.

subject: Pytest
question: Where is the code that captures failure screenshots for the pytest-html report?
explanation: pytest_runtest_makereport in conftest.py is the hook that intercepts test outcomes and attaches screenshots to the pytest-html report on failure.

subject: Pytest
question: Which conftest.py hook creates the environment details section inside the Allure report?
option_a: pytest_sessionfinish — runs after all tests complete and finalises environment info for Allure
option_c: pytest_configure — sets up report paths at session start
option_d: pytest_collection_modifyitems — filters test items before execution
explanation: pytest_sessionfinish fires once when the entire session ends, making it the right place to write environment metadata that Allure renders in its environment panel.

subject: Pytest
question: How is TDD applied in the context of this automation framework?
option_a: The test script step is written first (e.g., login_page.login(...)), which fails because the method does not exist yet; then the Page Object method is implemented to make it pass
option_b: Unit tests for every utility function are written before any utility code is created
option_c: Gherkin Given-When-Then scenarios are written before any Page Object is created
option_d: Test stubs are auto-generated from the application source code before manual refinement
explanation: The team adapts TDD to UI automation: write the test action call first, then build the Page Object method — ensuring the code is always written to satisfy a specific test requirement.

subject: Pytest
question: What Python naming style is used for class names in the framework?
explanation: PEP 8 specifies PascalCase for class names; the framework follows this with classes like BaseTest, BasePage, and LoginPage.

subject: Pytest
question: What naming convention is used for variables and function names in the framework?
explanation: PEP 8 mandates snake_case for functions and variables; this also makes pytest discover test_ prefixed functions automatically.

subject: Pytest
question: What naming convention is used for locators and constants in the framework?
explanation: UPPER_CASE signals that these are constants — locator tuples that should not be changed at runtime, following PEP 8 conventions.

subject: Pytest
question: What style guide do all naming conventions in the framework follow?
option_a: PEP 8 — the standard Python style guide
explanation: PEP 8 is the canonical Python style guide; the framework follows it for snake_case functions, PascalCase classes, and UPPER_CASE constants.

subject: Pytest
question: What is a virtual environment (venv) and why is it required for this framework?
option_a: An isolated directory with a specific Python version and all project libraries — ensuring everyone uses identical dependency versions and preventing conflicts
option_b: A cloud-based environment where Selenium tests run remotely on different browsers
option_c: A Docker container that packages the framework for cross-platform deployment
option_d: A Python namespace that prevents name collisions between different test modules
explanation: venv solves the 'works on my machine' problem by locking exact library versions for all developers and CI/CD servers.

subject: Pytest
question: How is the virtual environment activated on Windows?
explanation: On Windows the activate script is inside Scripts/; on macOS/Linux it is inside bin/ and requires the 'source' command.

subject: Pytest
question: What single command installs all framework dependencies after activating the venv?
option_c: pip install pytest selenium allure-pytest (one at a time)
explanation: requirements.txt lists every pinned dependency; pip install -r installs them all in one shot, guaranteeing version consistency.

subject: Pytest
question: What should a test script (test_*.py) deliberately NOT contain?
option_a: Raw Selenium code like driver.find_element() — all browser interactions must go through Page Object action methods
option_b: Assert statements — assertions belong only inside Page Object classes
option_c: @pytest.mark decorators — these should only be placed in conftest.py
option_d: Import statements — all imports must be centralised in __init__.py
explanation: Test scripts should be pure test logic (Arrange-Act-Assert); Selenium driver calls are encapsulated inside Page Objects to keep tests readable and maintainable.

subject: Pytest
question: What is the Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) pattern as applied in test scripts?
option_a: Arrange (initialise Page Objects), Act (call high-level action methods for the user journey), Assert (verify expected outcomes with assert)
option_b: Arrange (set up database state), Act (send API requests), Assert (validate HTTP response codes)
option_c: Arrange (write Gherkin steps), Act (run step definitions), Assert (check the Allure report)
option_d: Arrange (configure browser settings), Act (record Selenium IDE steps), Assert (replay and compare screenshots)
explanation: AAA keeps test scripts clean: Page Objects are wired up (Arrange), user flows are executed (Act), then outcomes are checked with Python's assert keyword (Assert).

subject: Pytest
question: What are the Allure decorators used for in test scripts?
option_a: @allure.feature, @allure.story, and @allure.title organise test results in the Allure report making it readable and navigable
option_b: @allure.fixture marks a function as an Allure-managed fixture with automatic screenshot capture
option_d: @allure.skip marks a test to be excluded from the Allure report but still executed
explanation: @allure.feature groups tests by application feature, @allure.story groups by user story, and @allure.title sets a human-readable test name in the report.

subject: Pytest
question: What is the difference between a decorator and a fixture in Pytest?
option_a: Decorators are labels/tags that describe HOW a test should run; fixtures are resources/services that provide the THINGS a test needs to run
option_b: Decorators provide setup and teardown logic; fixtures add metadata like markers to test functions
option_c: Decorators are only valid on class-based tests; fixtures only work on function-based tests
option_d: Decorators can be applied at most once per test; fixtures can be requested multiple times
explanation: @pytest.mark.smoke is a label (decorator); setup_and_teardown provides the driver (fixture). Decorators tag — fixtures supply.

subject: Pytest
question: What is the layered architecture of the framework from bottom to top?
option_a: Data Layer → Core Utilities Layer → Page Object Layer → Test Script Layer → Execution Layer → Reporting Layer
option_b: Browser Layer → Network Layer → Application Layer → Test Layer → Report Layer
option_c: Config Layer → Database Layer → API Layer → UI Layer → Test Layer
option_d: Requirements Layer → Design Layer → Coding Layer → Testing Layer → Deployment Layer
explanation: Each layer has a clear job: Data (Excel files), Utilities (reading/logging), POM (UI abstraction), Tests (logic), Execution (pytest+conftest), Reporting (Allure+pytest-html).

subject: Pytest
question: In the framework's execution flow, what is the correct sequence of events after running a pytest command?
option_a: pytest.ini read → conftest.py session setup → BaseTest creates browser → test runs Page Objects → failure handling → browser closed → reports finalised
option_b: config.yaml loaded → Page Objects initialised → all browsers launched → tests queued → results written
option_c: requirements.txt checked → venv activated → pytest.ini loaded → browsers launched in parallel → results streamed
option_d: conftest.py loads → pytest.ini read → test discovery → all fixtures initialised → batch execution
explanation: The flow: read pytest.ini for defaults → conftest.py session_logger fires → for each test, BaseTest's setup_and_teardown creates a browser → test calls Page Objects → on failure, evidence is captured → browser closed → Allure/HTML reports generated.

subject: Pytest
question: A developer adds a new Login page to the application. What must the QA engineer create first according to the POM architecture?
option_a: A new Python class in pages/ (e.g., login_page.py) inheriting from base_page.py, containing locators and a login() action method
option_b: A new test_*.py file directly containing driver.find_element() calls for the login form
option_c: A new entry in config.yaml listing the page's URL and element IDs as configuration values
option_d: A new row in the Excel data file specifying the page's test scenarios and credentials
explanation: POM dictates: page → class in pages/ inheriting BasePage. Only then does the test script call login_page.login(...) without any raw Selenium code.

subject: Pytest
question: A test fails on the CI server but cannot be reproduced locally. Where should the tester look first for evidence?
option_a: The timestamped log folder in logs/ and the failure screenshots automatically saved in reports/ by the framework
option_b: Re-run with -v flag and manually paste console output into a ticket
option_c: Open config.yaml and verify that the CI server's environment credentials are correct
option_d: Check requirements.txt to ensure all libraries are pinned to the correct versions
explanation: The framework automatically captures screenshots (reports/) and detailed step logs (logs/) for every failure, giving full post-mortem evidence without needing to reproduce.

subject: Pytest
question: A test needs to run with 10 different sets of login credentials stored in an Excel sheet. What is the correct implementation approach?
option_a: Use ExcelDataProvider to read the sheet as a list of dicts, then pass it to @pytest.mark.parametrize so Pytest runs the test once per row
option_b: Create 10 separate test functions each hardcoding one credential set directly in the test body
option_c: Add a for-loop inside a single test function iterating over a hardcoded list of tuples
option_d: Create 10 separate config.yaml files and run pytest once for each file
explanation: Data-driven testing via ExcelDataProvider + @pytest.mark.parametrize is the framework's standard pattern for multiple data sets — one test function, N executions.

subject: Pytest
question: A new developer joins the project and wants to run the framework locally. What is the correct setup order?
option_a: Clone repo → create venv → activate venv → pip install -r requirements.txt → run pytest
option_b: pip install pytest → clone repo → configure config.yaml → run pytest
option_c: Run pytest → identify missing packages from errors → install them one by one → re-run
option_d: Configure config.yaml first → install packages globally → clone repo → run pytest
explanation: The correct sequence ensures an isolated environment with all pinned dependencies before any test is executed.

subject: Pytest
question: The team notices intermittent 'stale element' failures when tests run in sequence. Which design decision in BaseTest prevents this type of cross-test contamination?
option_a: scope='function' on setup_and_teardown ensures each test gets a completely fresh browser instance, so DOM state from one test cannot affect another
option_b: scope='session' on session_logger ensures a single logging context shared by all tests
option_c: autouse=True on setup_and_teardown eliminates the need for explicit fixture injection
option_d: The DRY principle in base_page.py prevents locator strings from being duplicated across tests
explanation: Function-scoped browser setup is the key isolation mechanism — every test gets a new WebDriver instance, so cached DOM, session cookies, and stale elements from prior tests are gone.

subject: Pytest
question: A senior tester asks why screenshots for Allure and pytest-html are captured in two different files. What is the correct explanation?
option_a: pytest_runtest_makereport in conftest.py handles pytest-html screenshots; setup_and_teardown in base_test.py handles Allure screenshots — each report type requires its own capture hook
option_b: Both hooks capture screenshots identically; the difference is only where the files are stored
option_c: Allure captures screenshots automatically with no code needed; only pytest-html requires manual capture code
option_d: setup_and_teardown captures both types; conftest.py only handles log redirection
explanation: The two reporting plugins use different APIs: pytest_runtest_makereport uses the pytest-html 'extras' API; setup_and_teardown uses allure.attach() — each needs its own code.
